title: Deception datasets: application, high-interaction container, SCADA/IoT, keyword, custom service and file datasets, and CVE handlers

prose.label: Vulnerable application datasets.
prose.text: {{vulnerable-dataset-no-cve-needed}} {{vulnerable-dataset-handler-upload}} {{vulnerable-dataset-list-columns}} Whether the handler file name must match its CVE ID {{gap:handler-file-name}}.

checks.do: Whether a dataset is a default one before advising an edit or deletion.
Whether the files of a static application dataset zip sit at the archive root.
Whether a CVE handler declares CVE_ID as a string literal, routes async functions annotated -> Response and passes the validator.
Whether a web application container's port is final before saving, since changing it means uploading the docker image again.
Whether a protocol name is read from the protocol table or the datasets table, since the two label some protocols differently.

static-application-purpose.statement: Static application datasets configure the front ends of web applications deployed through TI decoys and network decoys via web services; they consist of static HTML, CSS and JavaScript files used to engage adversaries submitting credentials or attempting text-based web application attacks, and can be associated with dynamic or high-interaction applications to make responsive decoys.

quotes: Static application datasets allow you to configure the front ends of web applications that are deployed using Threat Intelligence (TI) decoys and network decoys via web services.

These datasets consist of static HTML files, CSS files, JavaScript files, etc. that can be used as an interface to engage adversaries submitting credentials or performing text-based web application attacks.
Creating responsive web application decoys by associating them with dynamic applications or high-interaction applications.

file-templates-page.statement: The File Templates page (Miragemaker > Files > File Templates) lists predefined and custom file templates, which are a baseline for file datasets; from it you can add a custom file template, download a file template, and edit or delete a file template.

quotes: Miragemaker file templates are a set of files that you can use as a baseline when creating file datasets.
On the File Templates page (Miragemaker > Files > File Templates), you can do the following:
View a list of predefined and custom file templates.
Add a custom file template.
Download a file template.
Edit or delete a file template.

application-dataset-kinds.statement: Application datasets are static (front ends of static HTML, CSS and JavaScript files), vulnerable application datasets (CVE datasets; requests and responses mimicking dynamic applications), dynamic (a static front end combined with a vulnerable dataset's interactions) and high-interaction container (docker-based) datasets, and the page describes deploying the datasets using TI decoys or web services on network decoys, and the custom protocol container page describes deploying that non-web container dataset as a network decoy.

quotes: which is a non-web application (e.g., PostgreSQL database server), and deploy it as a network decoy
see About Vulnerable Application Datasets (CVE Datasets)
Application datasets are resources used to build and deploy decoy web applications.
Static Application Datasets: Allows you to configure the front ends of web application decoys. These datasets consist of static HTML files, CSS files, JavaScript files, etc.
Vulnerable Application Datasets: Allows you to configure requests and responses to mimic dynamic web applications.
Dynamic Application Datasets: Combines appropriate front ends (static application datasets) and dynamic interactions (vulnerable application datasets) to create interactive decoy web applications.
High-Interaction Container Datasets: Self-contained docker container datasets that are fully interactive application decoys.
deploying the datasets using Threat Intelligence (TI) decoys or web services on network decoys

static-zip-root.statement: A static application dataset is uploaded as a .zip whose files must be at the root of the archive, not in a subdirectory.

quotes: you must create a compressed (.zip) file that includes the application dataset's files. The files must be present at the root of the zip file and not in a subdirectory.

static-dataset-fields.statement: A static application dataset has a web server banner, hostname keywords and subdomains (used by the Admin Portal to recommend hostnames and subdomains for decoys) and a MAC manufacturer.

quotes: Web Server Banner: Select a web server banner to advertise from the drop-down menu.
Hostname Keywords: Enter hostname keywords. The Zscaler Deception Admin Portal uses these keywords to recommend hostnames for decoys.
Subdomains: Enter subdomain names. The Deception Admin Portal uses these names to recommend subdomains for decoys.
MAC: Select a system manufacturer's name from the drop-down menu.

static-dataset-predefined.statement: Deception provides a few predefined static application datasets that can be used to deploy network decoys.

quotes: Zscaler Deception provides a few predefined static application datasets that you can readily use to deploy network decoys.

vulnerable-dataset-handler-upload.statement: A vulnerable application dataset requires a Python handler created beforehand and uploaded as a .py file no larger than 5 MB; vulnerability classification and CVE ID are optional.

quotes: Before you can add a vulnerable application dataset, you must create a Python handler.
Upload: Click to upload the custom CVE handler file (.py) for the vulnerable application. The file size cannot exceed 5 MB.
Vulnerability Classification: (Optional)
CVE ID: (Optional) Enter the CVE identifier

vulnerable-dataset-no-cve-needed.statement: Vulnerable application datasets are typically based on CVE disclosures but can also mimic any vulnerability, even without a CVE disclosure.

quotes: Typically, the requests and responses are created based on CVE disclosures for the specific application
you can also create custom requests and responses for dynamic web applications that mimic any vulnerability, even if there is no CVE disclosure for the vulnerability

vulnerable-dataset-list-columns.statement: The Vulnerable Application Datasets page lists Name, Vulnerability Classification, CVE ID, Linked Dynamic Applications and Description.

quotes: Name: The name of the vulnerable application dataset.
CVE ID: The CVE identifier associated with the publicly disclosed vulnerability configured in the application dataset.
Description: The description of the vulnerable application dataset.
Vulnerability Classification: The classification of the vulnerability mimicked by the vulnerable application dataset.
Linked Dynamic Applications: The list of all dynamic applications that are configured with the vulnerable application dataset.

dynamic-dataset-composition.statement: A dynamic application dataset takes a vulnerable application dataset for its dynamic interactions and, optionally, a fallback static application dataset to render the front-end UI, plus an optional web server banner.

quotes: Vulnerable Application Dataset: Select the vulnerable application dataset that must be used to configure the dynamic interactions of the application.
Fallback Static Application Dataset: (Optional) Select a static application dataset that must be used to render the front-end UI of the application.
Web Server Banner: (Optional) Select a web server banner

dynamic-dataset-uses.statement: Dynamic application datasets are used in TI decoys and network decoys, with the dynamic interactions configured through vulnerable application datasets and the front-end UI through associated static application datasets.

quotes: While the dynamic interactions are configured using Vulnerable Application Datasets, the front-end UI of the application is configured by associating appropriate Static Application Datasets.
Dynamic Application Datasets allow you to configure threat intelligence decoys and network decoys with dynamic web applications

hic-image-requirements.statement: A high-interaction container dataset is a single docker image holding all components the application needs, saved with docker save and compressed with gzip before upload; the ENTRYPOINT script must not exit or the service stops.

quotes: You must configure all the components required for the application in a single docker image, and then upload the image to the Zscaler Deception Admin Portal.
The ENTRYPOINT script must not exit. If it exits, the service stops.
docker save wordpress:latest > <image-name>
gzip <image-name>.tar

hic-image-example-commands.statement: The page's example for a docker container that runs a WordPress instance builds the image with docker build --tag <image-name> . and then saves it with docker save wordpress:latest > <image-name>.

quotes: A sample compressed file (.zip) includes the following components necessary to create a docker container that runs a WordPress instance:
In the command prompt, navigate to the directory where you have the files, and run the following commands:
docker build --tag <image-name> .
docker save wordpress:latest > <image-name>
For example, docker save wordpress:latest > myimage

hic-types-and-deployment.statement: High-interaction container datasets are Web (web application containers, deployable as TI or network decoys) or Custom (custom protocol containers for non-web applications such as a PostgreSQL server, deployed as network decoys).

quotes: Web indicates a web application container dataset and Custom indicates a custom protocol container dataset.
deploy it as a Threat Intelligence (TI) or network decoy
which is a non-web application (e.g., PostgreSQL database server), and deploy it as a network decoy

hic-port-immutable.statement: The port of a web application container dataset cannot be changed after saving; changing it requires deleting the container and uploading the docker image again.

quotes: The port details cannot be changed after you save the container configuration. If you want to change the port details, you must delete and upload the docker image file again.

hic-metrics-caveat.statement: Some high-interaction container datasets might capture fewer metrics than their static counterparts, because the request data format varies from application to application.

quotes: Each container runs a customized application, the format of the data sent in each request varies from application to application. Therefore, some high-interaction container datasets might capture fewer metrics than their static counterparts.

scada-protocols.statement: The SCADA/IoT page's table of supported protocols lists BACnet, DNP3, EtherNet/IP, Guardian AST, HTTP, IEC 60870-5-104, IEC 61850, IPMI, Kamstrup, Modbus, OPC UA, PROFINET, S7comm and SNMP.

quotes: | BACnet | Building automation and device control | Smart buildings |
| DNP3 | Telemetry and control | Power and water |
| EtherNet/IP | Industrial device communication | Manufacturing |
| Guardian AST | Asset monitoring and threat detection | Industrial security |
| HTTP | Web/API communication | Cross-industry |
| IEC 60870-5-104 | Telecontrol systems | Power utilities |
| IEC 61850 | Substation communication | Power grids |
| IPMI | Remote hardware management | Data centers |
| Kamstrup | Smart metering communication | Utilities |
| Modbus | PLS/RU communication | Industrial automation |
| OPC UA | System integration and data exchange | Cross-industry |

scada-protocol-labels.statement: The SCADA/IoT page labels two protocols differently in its two tables: the protocol table has IEC 60870-5-104 and Guardian AST, while the datasets table has a dataset named IEC 104 whose Protocols Supported column lists IEC 104, and a dataset named Guardian AST whose Protocols Supported column lists GUARDIAN_AST.

quotes: | Guardian AST | Asset monitoring and threat detection | Industrial security |
| IEC 60870-5-104 | Telecontrol systems | Power utilities |
evidence.after: View a table showing supported SCADA/IoT protocols.

quotes: | IEC 104 | IEC 104, DNP3, IEC 61850, and SNMP | Power/utility automation endpoint exposing IEC 104 along with related substation protocols |
| Guardian AST | GUARDIAN_AST | Tank monitoring endpoint for fuel inventory, level, temperature, and water measurements |
evidence.after: View a table showing supported SCADA/IoT datasets and their protocols.

scada-default-datasets.statement: Deception provides device-based datasets that mimic specific SCADA/IoT devices and protocol-based datasets that mimic generic SCADA/IoT devices, and custom datasets can be uploaded.

quotes: By default, Zscaler Deception provides a list of datasets that includes device-based datasets to mimic specific SCADA/IoT devices and protocol-based datasets to mimic generic SCADA/IoT devices. You can also create and upload custom SCADA/IoT datasets.

scada-dataset-example-multiprotocol.statement: The Building Automation - Siemens PLC dataset lists Modbus, OPC UA, PROFINET, S7comm, ENIP, BACnet, HTTP, IPMI and SNMP as its supported protocols.

quotes: | Building Automation - Siemens PLC | Modbus, OPC UA, PROFINET, S7comm, ENIP, BACnet, HTTP, IPMI, and SNMP |
evidence.after: View a table showing supported SCADA/IoT datasets and their protocols.

scada-custom-dataset-workflow.statement: A custom SCADA/IoT dataset is made by downloading an existing dataset as a .zip, changing it as needed, and uploading it under Dataset/Templates (Zip File); it is then used in network decoys.

quotes: Make the necessary changes to the SCADA/IoT dataset that you downloaded to meet your requirements.
Locate an existing SCADA/IoT dataset based on the new custom dataset you want to create, and click the Download icon.
The SCADA/IoT dataset (.zip) is downloaded to your system.
Dataset/Templates (Zip File): Click Upload to upload the custom dataset you saved to your system.
You can use the dataset in network decoys to deploy SCADA/IoT decoys.

keyword-recommendation-rules.statement: Configured keywords are included in addition to randomly generated recommendations; a keyword is part of the generated text and never used alone, only one keyword is used per recommendation, and with multiple keywords one is chosen randomly.

quotes: When keywords are configured, Zscaler generates recommendations that include the keywords in addition to randomly generated recommendations.
the keyword is part of the generated texts and is not exclusively used to avoid conflicts
if "admin" is a configured keyword, keyword-based recommendations can be admin-pc, adminlog, etc., and cannot be "admin" alone.
Only one keyword is used for each keyword-based recommendation.
when multiple keywords are configured, keywords are chosen randomly to generate a recommendation

keyword-config.statement: Keyword datasets take one keyword per line and are used to autogenerate recommendations for decoy parameters such as hostnames, file and folder names and network decoy names.

quotes: Enter keywords (one per line) of your choice.
autogenerate recommendations for decoy parameters, such as hostnames, file and folder names, network decoy names, etc.

custom-service-purpose.statement: A custom service dataset creates custom network services with customized requests and responses over any binary or text-based application-layer protocol, deployed through network decoys on a configured port and TCP or UDP.

quotes: A custom service dataset is a mechanism that creates custom network services with customized requests and responses.
The custom services can be created over any binary or text-based protocols in the application layer and can then be deployed using network decoys.
you can configure specific ports and network layer protocols (TCP or UDP)

custom-service-fields.statement: A custom service dataset has a Binary or Text protocol type and optional banner and default response; for binary protocols the banner, default response and request and response messages must be Base64-encoded text.

quotes: Protocol: Select the application layer protocol type (Binary or Text) that you want for your custom service.

Banner: (Optional) Enter the banner message that is shown to adversaries when a connection is established with the service using network decoys. For binary protocols, the value entered for this field must be a Base64-encoded text.
Default Response: (Optional) Enter the default response that is sent for unknown requests from adversaries. For binary protocols, the value entered for this field must be a Base64-encoded text.
For binary protocols, the values entered for request and response must be a Base64-encoded text.

file-dataset-static-dynamic.statement: A static file dataset gives each decoy an exact copy of its uploaded .zip files, while a dynamic file dataset generates a new set of files every time a decoy is deployed.

quotes: Each decoy configured with a static dataset contains an exact copy of the files in the static dataset.
you must have the required files in a compressed (.zip) file
Every time a decoy with a dynamic dataset is deployed, a new set of files is generated and then copied to the decoy.

file-dataset-dynamic-fields.statement: A dynamic file dataset is parameterised by file classification by department, file templates, custom keywords used in file name permutations, a minimum and maximum date, and folder and file-per-folder ranges used to randomly select a few folders and files each time an instance is generated for a decoy.

quotes: File Classification by Department:
File Templates: Select the type of decoy file you want to deploy from the drop-down menu
Custom Keywords: Enter the keywords you want to include for the industry type. These keywords are used in file name permutations.
Minimum Date and Maximum Date: Select the start and end date.

Minimum Folders and Maximum Folders: Enter the minimum and maximum numbers of folders. This range is used to randomly select a few folders every time an instance of a file dataset is generated for a decoy.

Minimum Files Per Folder and Maximum Files Per Folder: Enter the minimum and maximum files per folder. This range is used to randomly select a few files per folder every time an instance of a file dataset is generated for a decoy.

file-dataset-uses.statement: File datasets configure network decoys (services that host files, such as Shares and FTP) and landmine decoys, and a GenAI icon marks a generative AI file dataset.

quotes: File datasets are realistic-looking decoy files and folders that you can use to configure network and landmine decoys.
Network deception: Populate decoy services that host files, such as Shares and FTP.
Landmine deception: Configure decoy files that match a user or system profile.
The GenAI icon indicates a generative AI file dataset.

file-template-baseline.statement: A file template is uploaded as a .zip and is used as a baseline when adding dynamic file datasets.

quotes: You can add a custom file template and use it as a baseline when adding dynamic file datasets.
you must create a compressed (.zip) file that includes the template's files

default-datasets-readonly.statement: Default static application, vulnerable application, dynamic application, high-interaction container, SCADA/IoT, custom service and file datasets and file templates cannot be edited or deleted.

quotes: The default static application datasets cannot be edited.
The default static application datasets cannot be deleted.
The default vulnerable application datasets cannot be edited.
The default vulnerable application datasets cannot be deleted.
The default dynamic application datasets cannot be edited.
The default dynamic application datasets cannot be deleted.
The default high-interaction containers cannot be edited.
The default high-interaction containers cannot be deleted.
The default SCADA/IoT datasets cannot be edited.
The default SCADA/IoT datasets cannot be deleted.
The default custom service datasets cannot be edited.
The default custom service datasets cannot be deleted.
The default file datasets cannot be edited.
The default file datasets cannot be deleted.
The default file templates cannot be edited.
The default file templates cannot be deleted.

download-formats.statement: Static application, vulnerable application, SCADA/IoT and file datasets and file templates, both default and custom, download individually as a ZIP file.

quotes: You can download both default and custom static application datasets individually as a ZIP file.
You can download both default and custom vulnerable application datasets individually as a ZIP file.
You can download both default and custom SCADA/IoT datasets individually as a ZIP file.
You can download both default and custom file datasets individually as a ZIP file.
You can download both default and custom file templates individually as a ZIP file.

handler-location-and-validation.statement: A CVE handler is a Python file that teaches a decoy how to respond to exploit attempts targeting a specific vulnerability; each lives at datasets/aicve/<CVE-ID>.py and is validated by an AST parser before upload.

quotes: A CVE handler is a Python file that teaches a decoy how to respond to exploit attempts targeting a specific vulnerability.
Each handler file lives at datasets/aicve/<CVE-ID>.py and is validated by an AST parser before it can be uploaded.

handler-required-pieces.statement: A handler file requires three top-level pieces: a CVE_ID string constant, one or more async handler functions, and a ROUTES list; imports, constants and helper functions are allowed and not inspected.

quotes: CVE_ID: A string constant identifying the vulnerability.
One or more handler functions (async functions) that accept a request and return a response.
ROUTES: A list that maps HTTP methods and URL paths to your handler functions.
Beyond these pieces, you can add imports, constants, and helper functions as needed.
The validator only inspects the required pieces.

handler-cve-id-literal.statement: CVE_ID must be a plain string literal at module level, not computed from a function call, read from a file or defined inside a conditional block.

quotes: Assign CVE_ID as a plain string literal at the module level. It cannot be computed from a function call, read from a file, or defined inside a conditional block.

handler-function-rules.statement: Each routed handler function must be declared async def, accept exactly one argument (the Starlette Request object) and be annotated -> Response, although any Starlette response subclass can be returned at runtime.

quotes: Async: Declared with async def, not plain def.
Single-parameter: Accepts exactly one argument (the Starlette Request object).
Annotated with -> Response and the return type must be Response.
At runtime, you can return any Starlette response subclass (PlainTextResponse, HTMLResponse, etc.), but the annotation must say Response.

handler-routes-rules.statement: ROUTES is a module-level list literal of dicts each with METHOD (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH, HEAD or OPTIONS), PATH (a string literal starting with /, supporting Starlette path parameters) and HANDLER (a bare function reference); duplicate method and path pairs in one file are rejected.

quotes: ROUTES must be a list literal assigned at the module level.
METHOD: A string literal. Must be GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH, HEAD, or OPTIONS.
PATH: A string literal starting with /. Supports Starlette path parameters like {id} or {rest:path}.
HANDLER: A bare reference to one of your async handler functions
Duplicate routes (same method and path) within a single handler file are rejected.

handler-unrouted-ignored.statement: A function not referenced in ROUTES is ignored by the validator, which checks only CVE_ID, ROUTES and the functions referenced by ROUTES.

quotes: If a function is not referenced in ROUTES, the validator ignores it entirely. Only routed handlers are checked.
It only checks CVE_ID, ROUTES, and the functions referenced by ROUTES.

handler-path-params.statement: A {name} path segment matches a single path component and {name:path} matches everything including slashes; captured values are read through request.path_params.

quotes: A {name} segment matches a single path component, while {name:path} matches everything including slashes.
access captured values through request.path_params

handler-session-store.statement: Handlers get an in-memory session store at request.state.sessions with async create(data, ttl=300), get(key), set(key, data, ttl=300) and delete(key) methods; its data is lost on decoy restart.

quotes: Access it via request.state.sessions. It provides 4 async methods:
create(data={...}, ttl=300): Creates a new session and returns a UUID key.
get(key): Retrieves session data, or None if expired or missing.
set(key, data, ttl=300): Stores data under a specific key.
delete(key): Removes a session.
All data lives in memory and is lost on the decoy restart, which is by design for decoy interactions.

handler-validator-run.statement: The handler validator is downloaded as TXT, renamed to .py and run with python3 <validator>.py --file-path <handler>.py, printing OK: <file> on success or FAIL: <error-message> on failure.

quotes: The validator file is downloaded in TXT format.
Rename the file by changing the extension from .txt to .py.
python3 <validator-file-name>.py --file-path <handler-file-name>.py
OK: <handler-file-name>.py
FAIL: <error-message>

handler-validation-errors.statement: Validator errors include 'Handler must assign CVE_ID as a string', 'Handler must define ROUTES as a list literal', 'ROUTES entry N: duplicate route', and handler must accept exactly 1 parameter and have return type annotation -> Response.

quotes: Handler must assign CVE_ID as a string: Either CVE_ID is missing, or it's assigned to something other than a string literal
Handler must define ROUTES as a list literal: Either ROUTES is missing, or it's assigned to something other than a [...] list expression.
ROUTES entry N: duplicate route "GET /path": Another entry in the same file already uses this exact method and path combination.
ROUTES entry N: handler "X" must accept exactly 1 parameter: The function takes zero or more than one argument.
ROUTES entry N: handler "X" must have return type annotation -> Response: The function is missing a return type annotation, or the annotation is something other than Response.

handler-file-name.title: Whether a handler file's name must match its CVE ID
handler-file-name.detail: The handler page says each handler file lives at datasets/aicve/<CVE-ID>.py, while the vulnerable application dataset upload step takes any .py file; neither says whether the name must match.

zip-upload-limits.title: Size limits for dataset and template zip uploads
zip-upload-limits.detail: Only the 5 MB .py handler limit is stated; the pages read give no size limit for the zip uploads of static application datasets, SCADA/IoT datasets, file datasets or file templates.

scada-dataset-rows.title: The remaining rows of the SCADA/IoT datasets table
scada-dataset-rows.detail: The table of datasets and their supported protocols has 28 rows; only the Building Automation - Siemens PLC row and the two labelled rows are recorded.
